lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Meal Planning, Cooking, and Food Management
lessonRef.title: Correction and reflection: cleanup and food-waste reduction

objective: Learners review a short food-waste observation log or a cleanup routine, identify one specific recurring habit that causes waste or leaves cleanup incomplete, and revise that one habit with a concrete replacement, explaining why the change should reduce waste or improve cleanup.
scenario: Looking back over the past few days of meals in the household, the learner records what got thrown away or left half-finished and why, or walks through the usual after-meal cleanup routine step by step, and then picks the single habit most responsible for waste or an incomplete cleanup and rewrites it into a specific new habit to try next week.
materials: memory of recent meals or the household's usual cleanup routine

tasks.directions: Think back over the last several meals before writing anything down.

prompts.text: List two or three specific things that were thrown away, left uneaten, or forgotten in the refrigerator recently, naming the actual food each time.

tasks.directions: Walk through the household's usual after-meal cleanup routine step by step, in the order it actually happens, and note where it tends to break down or get skipped.

prompts.text: I listed the cleanup routine in the actual order it happens, not the order it should happen.
I marked the specific step where cleanup most often gets skipped or rushed.

tasks.directions: Choose the single habit, either from the food-waste list or the cleanup routine, that causes the most repeated waste or the most incomplete cleanup. Rewrite that one habit into a specific, doable replacement you could actually start next week, and explain exactly why the new version should reduce waste or leave the kitchen more finished than the old habit did.

prompts.text: Name the one habit you are changing, describe the specific replacement habit, and explain why this particular change should reduce waste or improve cleanup rather than just being a general good intention.

tasks.directions: Consider what would make the new habit realistic to keep.

prompts.text: What is the most likely reason this new habit could fail to stick after a week, and what would help you notice if it was slipping?

remediation: If a learner names a habit change that is too vague to act on (for example, 'waste less food' or 'clean up better'), reteach by asking two follow-up questions together (what exactly would you do differently, and when specifically would you do it) and having the learner rewrite the habit as one concrete action tied to a specific moment.
extension: Have the learner try the new habit for three real days, keep a short log of whether it happened each day, and write a short follow-up on whether the habit reduced waste or improved cleanup as predicted.
